title: Emotions and moods
subtitle: on cloud nine, down in the dumps, scared stiff
summary: Understand the fixed expressions English uses for happiness, bad moods, illness and fear.

lesson.heading: Positive feelings and moods
lesson.text: These are fixed expressions - you cannot change the words in them. They all describe someone who is happy or cheerful.

examples.text: Maria seems to be **on cloud nine** these days.
Everyone seemed to be **in high spirits**.
She seems to be **keeping her chin up**.

examples.note: as happy as can be and as happy as the day is long mean the same: extremely content

lesson.heading: Negative feelings and moods
rows: look or feel depressed or sad
be **like a bear with a sore head**

lesson.heading: Negative moods in sentences
lesson.text: Notice which verb each expression takes: you **have** a long face, you **are** down in the dumps, and you **throw** a wobbly.

examples.text: What's the matter? You've got **a long face**.
She certainly looked **down in the dumps**.
It's been an awful day, so no wonder Zac is **in a bad mood**.
Martin was **like a bear with a sore head** all morning.
Alice **threw a wobbly** the other day.

lesson.heading: Physical feelings and states
rows: not very well: You're looking a bit **under the weather**.
in very good physical condition: She looked, and felt, **on top form**.
unable to balance, as if you will fall over: I suddenly felt my head was **spinning**.
very ill indeed: I was almost **at death's door** last week!
very fit indeed: Old Nora's **as fit as a fiddle**.

lesson.heading: Fear and fright
lesson.text: English has many exaggerated ways of saying you were frightened. **Scared stiff** and **scared out of your wits** describe your own fear; **frighten the life out of somebody** describes what another person does to you.

examples.text: The poor lad was **scared out of his wits**.
She **frightened the life out of** him.
We were all **shaking in our boots**.
examples.note: shaking in our shoes is also possible: trembling with fear

examples.text: I **jumped out of my skin** when I heard the bang.
examples.note: = gave a big jump from shock

lesson.heading: More expressions for reactions
rows: deal calmly with events as they happen
feel very proud because of something good you did

lesson.heading: Using them naturally
lesson.text: Here they are in context, from a horoscope column - exactly the kind of informal writing where such expressions belong.

examples.text: Don't **get carried away** by promises that are not kept.
**Keep a cool head** and **take everything as it comes**.
On the work front, things are **looking up**.
If someone says something that makes you **swell with pride** and feel **on top of the world**, enjoy the moment!

lesson.text: There is often an element of exaggeration in these expressions - they lighten the tone of what you are saying. Use them only in informal situations.

exercises.prompt: Match the beginning of each fixed expression with its ending.

pairs.right: happy as the day is long
a bear with a sore head

exercises.prompt: Has something good happened? You all seem in ___.
exercises.explanation: Be in high spirits = be lively and enjoying things.

exercises.prompt: What's the matter? You've got a long ___.
exercises.explanation: Have a long face = look depressed or sad.

exercises.prompt: Has something bad happened? You look down ___.
exercises.explanation: Be down in the dumps = look or feel depressed.

exercises.prompt: As long as he has his car to work on, he's as happy as ___.
exercises.explanation: As happy as Larry = extremely content. As happy as can be means the same.

exercises.prompt: Match what each person says with the expression that describes them.

pairs.left: Lidia: I was just not feeling very well yesterday.
Karen: I've gone to the gym every day this month and I can feel the results.
Mark: I've never felt so terrified in my life.
Lars: I was very ill indeed last week.
Andrea: I felt as if I couldn't keep my balance.
Krishnan: I've been feeling really well recently.

exercises.prompt: I gave a sudden jump when he fired the gun. I ___ when he fired the gun.
exercises.explanation: Jump out of your skin = give a big jump from shock.

exercises.prompt: I think you should not panic and just be patient. I think you should ___ and just be patient.
exercises.explanation: Keep a cool head = stay calm.

exercises.prompt: He scared me very much when he came in wearing that ghost mask! He ___ me when he came in wearing that ghost mask!
exercises.explanation: Frighten the life out of somebody = frighten them a lot.

exercises.prompt: Everyone was trembling with fear when they saw the door open all by itself. Everyone was ___.
options: like a bear with a sore head
exercises.explanation: Shake in your boots (or shoes) = tremble with fear.

exercises.prompt: She felt very proud indeed as her daughter received the gold medal. She ___ as her daughter received the gold medal.
exercises.explanation: Swell with pride = feel very pleased because of something good that happened.

exercises.prompt: Does each expression describe a happy person or an unhappy, bad-tempered one?

items.text: like a bear with a sore head

exercises.statement: I was scared stiff before I did the bungee jump, but it was OK.
exercises.explanation: Correct. Scared stiff = very scared. Scared out of my wits would also work here.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order. You got too excited about joining a rock band.
exercises.answer: I think I got carried away by the idea
exercises.explanation: Get carried away = get too excited.

exercises.prompt: I try to just deal with events in a calm way as they happen. I try to just ___.
exercises.explanation: Take everything as it comes = deal calmly with events as they happen.
